lesson.title: Turning Vibrating Air Into Sound
lesson.summary: Hearing converts physical sound waves into neural signals through a precise mechanical chain in the ear, and the extraordinary sensitivity of that system is what makes the absolute threshold for faint sounds so low.
lesson.body:
Sound begins as vibrations traveling through the air as waves, and the ear's job is to capture those vibrations and convert them into neural activity the brain can interpret. The outer ear, including the visible pinna and the ear canal, funnels sound waves toward the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates in response to the incoming pressure changes. Those vibrations then pass into the middle ear, a small air filled cavity containing three tiny bones, commonly called the hammer, anvil, and stirrup, which form a mechanical lever system that amplifies the vibrations before passing them along to the inner ear.

The inner ear contains the cochlea, a fluid filled, coiled structure shaped roughly like a snail shell. Vibrations transmitted into the cochlea create waves in its fluid, which in turn move the basilar membrane, a structure running the length of the cochlea lined with thousands of specialized hair cells. As the basilar membrane moves, these hair cells bend, and that bending triggers the release of neurotransmitters, converting mechanical vibration into neural signals, a form of transduction just like the process by which the retina converts light into neural signals in vision. Those signals then travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound.

Two complementary theories explain how the auditory system encodes pitch, or how high or low a sound seems. Place theory proposes that different frequencies of sound cause peak vibration at different specific locations along the basilar membrane, with high frequencies producing peak activity near the base of the cochlea and low frequencies producing peak activity farther along, so pitch is partly encoded by which hair cells are most active. Frequency theory proposes that the basilar membrane, and the neurons connected to it, can also fire at a rate that directly matches the frequency of the incoming sound wave for lower pitches, providing the brain with a second, timing based code for pitch. Because neither theory fully explains the whole range of audible pitches on its own, most current understanding treats them as complementary, with place theory better explaining higher frequencies and frequency theory better explaining lower ones.

The extraordinary mechanical sensitivity of this system connects directly back to Absolute Threshold. Just as rods in the retina can respond to remarkably small amounts of light, the hair cells of the cochlea can respond to vibrations so minute that a ticking watch across a silent room, the classic illustration of an auditory absolute threshold, can trigger a detectable neural signal. This sensitivity comes at a cost, though, since hair cells can be permanently damaged by exposure to very loud sounds and do not regenerate in humans, which is why hearing loss from repeated loud noise exposure is typically irreversible.
